paragraphs.heading: Landforms and forces together
paragraphs.text: Coastal morphodynamics studies how coastal landforms and physical processes interact. The processes include waves, tides, currents, wind, the transport of sediment and severe weather events. Shorelines evolve over both short and long timescales, through changes that are gradual and changes that come in episodes. The factors that influence these changes are interconnected, and local geology and environmental conditions are among them.

paragraphs.heading: How the coast is studied
paragraphs.text: Researchers in this field rely on observations, practical models and computer models. With them they analyze the coastal environment and try to anticipate how it will change. Coastal landforms such as estuaries and sand dunes were observed in the field, to document how sediment is transported and what form the shoreline takes. From this came a basic conceptual model that ties together the interconnected factors behind coastal evolution. The conclusions of the field give insight into what shapes coastlines and into how human activity affects coastal systems.

paragraphs.heading: Why a beach is always catching up
paragraphs.text: The moving water responds instantly when the form of the coast changes. The form of the coast cannot answer as quickly, because changing it means redistributing sediment. Sediment needs a finite time to move, so the response of the landform lags behind the forcing of the water. The conditions that drive the water change regularly. As a result, the affected beach never reaches equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: Flat beaches and steep beaches
paragraphs.text: Beaches can be dissipative or reflective. A dissipative beach is wide and flat and is made of fine sand. Its waves tend to break a long way from the intertidal zone and lose their force bit by bit across a wide surf zone. A reflective beach is steep and is known for coarse sand. It has no surf zone, and its waves break abruptly on the intertidal zone.

paragraphs.heading: How a beach changes state
paragraphs.text: Coarser sediment lets water percolate through it during the swash part of the wave cycle. That weakens the backwash and lets material be deposited in the swash zone. Beaches also move from one state to another, and a change in wave energy is often the cause. Storms flatten the profile of a reflective beach, as steeper waves move sediment offshore. The beach then takes on a more dissipative profile.

paragraphs.heading: Currents near the seabed
paragraphs.text: Currents near the bottom vary with the state of the beach. Where a beach is reflective, the dominant motions are incident waves and subharmonic edge waves. Some beaches are in intermediate states, with pronounced topographies of bars and troughs. The strongest rips, and the feeder currents that go with them, occur with intermediate topographies of transverse bars and rips.
